sections.heading: The challenger playbook: bare metal and flat networks
bullets: A latecomer cloud cannot out-scale the incumbents, so it competes on architecture: bare-metal servers hand customers the physical machine with no virtualization layer — eliminating the 'hypervisor tax' of performance lost to software that shares hardware among tenants

Flat, non-oversubscribed networks are the second move: traditional clouds oversubscribe — selling more potential bandwidth than the wires can carry at once, betting users won't all peak together — but AI training peaks everything simultaneously, so the challenger builds for worst case

Lateness becomes an asset when the workload changes: a network and data-center design conceived after AI training defined the requirements carries no legacy compromises, while the incumbent's decade of general-purpose optimization becomes baggage

The playbook's limit is breadth: architecture wins the compute-intensive tenant but not the enterprise that needs hundreds of managed services — which is why challengers pair the AI niche with whatever franchise they already own

sections.heading: Data gravity: why the database anchors everything
bullets: Data behaves like mass: applications, analytics, and now AI models must run near the data they use, because moving petabytes is slow, risky, and expensive — so wherever an enterprise's core records sit exerts gravitational pull on every other workload

Egress fees amplify the physics: clouds charge to move data out but not in — an asymmetry that makes an accumulated data estate progressively more expensive to leave, and a pricing structure competition regulators increasingly examine

The database vendor holds a privileged position: decades of mission-critical records — finance, inventory, customers — live in its formats, tuned by its tools, run by staff trained on its stack; replatforming a core database is among the riskiest projects in enterprise IT

AI raises the stakes: models are most valuable operating on a company's own data, so 'where can AI securely reach the database' becomes a cloud-selection criterion — gravity that a database incumbent can convert into infrastructure revenue

sections.heading: Multicloud: selling inside your rival's building
bullets: Multicloud interconnection links two clouds' data centers with dedicated private fiber so a workload can split across them — the database in one, the application in the other — with latency low enough that the seam barely shows

The bolder version embeds outright: the vendor installs its own racks inside a rival cloud's data centers and sells its database as a native service there — rivals cooperate because each keeps the slice of customer spend it would otherwise lose entirely

Latency decides what is possible: a chatty application making thousands of round trips to its database tolerates microseconds, not the milliseconds between distant facilities — which is why embedding hardware beats interconnecting buildings for the tightest workloads

Strategically, multicloud converts a defensive position into distribution: the player too small to win the whole cloud account instead rides its anchor product into every rival's cloud — interoperability as market access rather than concession

sections.heading: The GPU landlord: leasing superclusters to AI labs
bullets: A compute landlord signs a multi-year lease for GPU capacity with an AI lab, then builds the data centers against that signature — importing commercial real estate logic: anchor tenants, long leases, and construction financed against contracted rent

Margins are structurally thin: renting hardware anyone can buy earns rental-market returns — reported analyses put GPU-rental gross margins near 15% versus roughly 70% for proprietary software — so the landlord profits on volume and financing spread, not product differentiation

Concentration is the defining risk: when one tenant dominates the order book, the landlord's creditworthiness becomes a derivative of the tenant's — lenders end up pricing the landlord's bonds off a customer whose audited financials they may never see

Contracted-backlog figures need careful reading: signed commitments convert to cash only as capacity is delivered and the tenant actually pays over years — announced backlog measures ambition and trust; delivered, collected revenue measures the business

sections.heading: RDMA and the storage that feeds training
bullets: Remote direct memory access (RDMA) lets one server's network card read or write another server's memory directly, bypassing both operating systems — cutting communication latency from milliseconds toward microseconds and freeing processors from shuffling packets

Training runs on synchronized exchanges: thousands of GPUs repeatedly share updates and the whole cluster waits on the slowest message — which is why AI fabrics are built on RDMA-class networking rather than ordinary internet protocols

Feeding the GPUs is a storage problem: training data streams from network-attached storage — shared disk farms reached over the fabric — through parallel file systems that stripe every file across many machines so thousands of simultaneous readers never queue behind one

Checkpointing is storage's second job: training state is saved periodically so a failure costs hours instead of months — and writing terabytes fast enough that the cluster isn't idling makes burst write bandwidth a hidden determinant of effective compute

sections.heading: Capex-on-demand: building only what's already sold
bullets: Two ways to build infrastructure: speculative construction hopes demand appears after the concrete cures; contracted construction breaks ground only once a signed commitment covers the asset — trading upside and speed for far lower risk of stranded capital

It is the pre-leasing discipline from real estate: developers who secure anchor tenants before pouring foundations survive the downturns that bankrupt speculative peers — applied to compute, no data hall starts without a lease behind it

The model shifts risk rather than removing it: stranded-asset risk becomes counterparty risk — the builder is protected from absent demand but exposed to the single customer whose contract justified the build failing to pay

How to read a capex-on-demand company: capital spending growth should trail contracted-backlog growth, and financing raised should map to signed deals — capex accelerating ahead of contracts is the tell that the discipline is quietly eroding

flashcards.q: What is the 'hypervisor tax' and how does bare metal avoid it?
flashcards.a: The hypervisor is the software layer that shares one physical server among tenants — it costs performance and adds variability. Bare metal hands the customer the whole physical machine with no virtualization layer, delivering full, predictable performance — a selling point when the workload is a GPU cluster running flat-out.

flashcards.q: What does it mean that a cloud network is 'oversubscribed', and why does AI training break that bet?
flashcards.a: Oversubscription sells more potential bandwidth than the wires can carry at once, wagering that customers won't all peak together — usually true for web workloads. Synchronized AI training makes every GPU transmit simultaneously by design, so a challenger built with non-oversubscribed, worst-case networking wins that tenant.

The tendency of applications, analytics, and AI to accumulate wherever the data already sits, because moving petabytes is slow, expensive, and risky. An enterprise's core database becomes an anchor that pulls every adjacent workload — and cloud decision — toward it.

flashcards.q: How do egress fees reinforce data gravity?
flashcards.a: Clouds charge for moving data out but not in, so a growing data estate becomes progressively more expensive to leave. The asymmetry converts physics-based friction into pricing-based lock-in — which is why competition regulators keep examining it.

flashcards.q: Why is replatforming a core enterprise database so rare?
flashcards.a: Decades of mission-critical records live in the incumbent's formats, tuned by its tools, operated by staff trained on its stack — and an error touches finance, inventory, and customers at once. The risk-reward is so unfavorable that most enterprises pay the incumbent indefinitely rather than migrate.

flashcards.q: Why would rival clouds let a competitor install racks inside their data centers?
flashcards.a: Because each keeps the slice of spend it would otherwise lose entirely: the customer wants that vendor's database and the host cloud's other services together. Embedding also solves the latency problem — chatty database traffic needs microseconds, which two distant clouds connected by fiber can't deliver.

flashcards.q: In the GPU-landlord model, what plays the role of real estate's anchor tenant?
flashcards.a: The AI lab whose multi-year lease justifies construction: financing is raised against its contracted payments the way a mall is financed against its anchor store's lease. The landlord's creditworthiness becomes a derivative of that tenant's ability to pay.

flashcards.q: Why are GPU-rental margins so much thinner than software margins?
flashcards.a: The landlord rents hardware anyone can buy — differentiation is limited, and the tenant knows the equipment's price. Reported analyses put GPU-rental gross margins near 15% versus roughly 70% for proprietary software; the rental business earns on volume and financing spread, not pricing power.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between announced backlog and actual business?
flashcards.a: Backlog is signed future commitments; it converts to cash only as capacity gets built, delivered, and paid for over years. It measures ambition and customer trust. Delivered, collected revenue measures the business — and the gap between the two is execution and counterparty risk.

flashcards.q: What is RDMA and why do AI fabrics require it?
flashcards.a: Remote direct memory access lets a network card read or write another server's memory directly, bypassing both operating systems — microsecond-class latency instead of milliseconds. Training synchronizes thousands of GPUs repeatedly and waits on the slowest message, so ordinary networking would leave the whole cluster idling.

flashcards.q: What do parallel file systems and checkpointing do for a training cluster?
flashcards.a: A parallel file system stripes every file across many storage machines so thousands of GPUs can read simultaneously without queueing. Checkpointing periodically saves training state so a failure loses hours, not months — and the burst write speed of those saves quietly determines how much compute you actually get.

flashcards.q: What is capex-on-demand, and what signals that the discipline is slipping?
flashcards.a: Building infrastructure only against signed customer commitments — real estate's pre-leasing rule applied to compute. It swaps stranded-asset risk for counterparty risk. The warning sign: capital spending accelerating faster than contracted backlog, meaning concrete is being poured on hope again.
